title: Will the Trump-Xi summit make limited progress on AI?
gist: Ahead of the September 24 Trump-Xi summit, PIIE's Alan Wm. Wolff argues trade, environmental, and geopolitical issues (Taiwan, Ukraine, Iran) will see only continuity of an uneasy truce, while AI safety is the one area with a real, if narrow, opening for US-China cooperation given industry leaders' warnings about near-term extinction-level risk and Trump's simultaneous dismissal of AI-safety concerns as a "hoax."

themes.theme: Summit expectations: trade and geopolitics stay frozen

insights.claim: Expectations for the September 24, 2026 Trump-Xi summit are low, with age, temperament, and entrenched strategic positions on both sides pointing to continued rivalry rather than major policy shifts.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Markets should not price in a major US-China trade or geopolitical breakthrough from this summit; the realistic base case is continuity of the status quo.
insights.quote: Expectations for the upcoming September 24 summit meeting in Washington between Presidents Xi Jinping of China and Donald Trump are not high.
insights.locator: opening paragraph

insights.claim: The most likely trade outcome is an extension of the trade truce reached at Busan the prior year, with Trump keeping a base tariff above 10% on China and retaining flexibility to impose selective import limits.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A base case of tariff-truce extension (not escalation or resolution) argues against positioning for either a trade-war re-escalation shock or a broad tariff-relief rally around the summit.
insights.quote: More likely than not the trade truce reached last year at Busan will be extended... Trump has no intention of abandoning a base tariff of something above 10 percent
insights.locator: trade and geopolitics section

insights.claim: China is expected to continue restricting access to choke-point commodities such as rare earths, critical minerals, and potentially active pharmaceutical ingredients as leverage in the trade relationship.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Continued Chinese chokehold risk on rare earths and APIs argues for sustained US/allied reshoring and stockpiling premiums in those supply chains regardless of summit outcome.
insights.quote: China will not surrender the option of providing only uncertain access for choke point commodities, e.g., rare earths and critical minerals, and at some point, perhaps, active pharmaceutical ingredients
insights.locator: trade and geopolitics section

insights.claim: The US is expected to keep export controls in place on high-end chips, semiconductor production equipment, and software as a matter of national security regardless of summit outcomes.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Persistent chip and semiconductor-equipment export controls sustain the investment case for non-China-exposed chip supply chains and for Chinese domestic semiconductor self-sufficiency efforts.
insights.quote: Nor can he credibly pledge to refrain from all national security export controls on high end chips, semiconductor production equipment, and software.
insights.locator: trade and geopolitics section

insights.claim: No breakthroughs are expected at the summit on environmental issues (climate change, overfishing, plastic pollution), pandemic preparedness, or expanded trade-discipline talks on subsidies and tariff transparency.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Global-commons issues will remain unaddressed by great-power coordination for at least another cycle, keeping the burden on smaller multilateral or regional efforts.
insights.quote: all environmental issues (e.g., climate change, overfishing, plastic pollution in the oceans) are areas that will remain unattended to
insights.locator: environmental and geopolitical section

insights.claim: Xi could be tempted toward a more aggressive approach on Taiwan reunification given the US Navy's commitment to the Strait of Hormuz, depleted US weapons stocks, and Washington's domestic focus on fuel prices.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: This is a live tail-risk flag: US naval overextension in the Middle East plus depleted munitions stocks is presented as a window of opportunity for Chinese assertiveness on Taiwan, relevant to defense and Taiwan-exposed supply-chain risk premia.
insights.quote: Xi could be tempted to take a more aggressive approach to reunification by the fact that the US Navy is tied down in the Strait of Hormuz and not deployed heavily in Asia, by US weapons stocks being depleted, and by Washington's attention being concentrated on fuel prices at the pump.
insights.locator: environmental and geopolitical section

insights.claim: US support for Taiwan is characterized as no more reliable right now than US commitment to NATO Article 5, given Trump's ambiguous public statements on the island's future.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A credibility discount on both Taiwan and NATO Article 5 commitments implies allies and markets should price higher geopolitical tail risk into Taiwan-adjacent assets (semiconductors, regional currencies) than official alliance rhetoric suggests.
insights.quote: US support for Taiwan is no more reliable than its commitment to Article 5 of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) right now, meaning not very.
insights.locator: environmental and geopolitical section

themes.theme: AI safety as the one live opening for cooperation

insights.claim: AI safeguards are identified as the one area where near-term US-China cooperation remains a real, open possibility, in contrast to trade and geopolitical issues where continuity is the base case.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: AI-safety dialogue is the summit's one genuine surprise-upside catalyst to watch, distinct from the priced-in continuity elsewhere.
insights.quote: One area of cooperation remains an open door—artificial intelligence (AI) safeguards.
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Leading AI company CEOs and engineers have forecast a meaningful chance of relatively near-term human extinction from AI escaping control.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Extinction-risk forecasts from the industry's own leadership are being used to justify treating AI safeguards as a first-order geopolitical priority, not a niche regulatory topic.
insights.quote: chances of relatively near-term human extinction have been forecast by leading AI company CEOs and engineers
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has reportedly been working on limited AI-safety engagement with China, but his approach focuses narrowly on risk prevention and preserving US technological lead rather than collaborative global regulation.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A US posture of 'narrow risk prevention plus lead preservation' rather than genuine collaborative regulation caps how far any summit AI announcement is likely to go.
insights.quote: Bessent's "approach focuses strictly on narrow risk prevention and maintaining the US technological lead, rather than collaborative global regulations."
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei published a 3,800-word essay, "We Must Pace the Frontier," calling for a global slowdown in AI development, endorsed by Sam Altman, Elon Musk, and Demis Hassabis.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Cross-lab CEO endorsement (Anthropic, OpenAI, xAI/SpaceX, Google DeepMind) of a slowdown essay signals unusual industry consensus that could translate into real policy momentum if channeled into the summit.
insights.quote: Dario Amodei, CEO of Anthropic, has recently published a 3,800-word essay, entitled We Must Pace the Frontier, calling for a global slowdown in AI development... endorsed by Sam Altman... Elon Musk... and... Demis Hassabis
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Chief scientists at OpenAI (Jakub Pachocki), Google DeepMind (Shane Legg), and Meta AI (Shengjia Zhao) have separately warned that no one is prepared for runaway AI.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Independent warnings from chief scientists at three separate labs (not just Anthropic) about unpreparedness for runaway AI reinforces that the extinction-risk concern is not a single-firm marketing position.
insights.quote: He is joined in expressing concerns by Jakub Pachocki, chief scientist at OpenAI, who has repeatedly warned that no one is prepared for runaway AI, as did Shane Legg, chief AGI scientist at Google DeepMind, and Shengjia Zhao, chief scientist at Meta AI.
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Amodei's proposal lays out four escalating levels of US-China AI cooperation: curbing dangerous uses like bioweapons development, pre-release model testing on cybersecurity/biology/alignment risks, a 'speed limit' on recursive self-improvement, and a full pacing or pause on overall AI development.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: This four-level framework is a concrete negotiating ladder to watch for at the summit or in follow-on talks — even reaching level 1 (curbing bioweapon-enabling uses) would be a meaningful signal.
insights.quote: Amodei suggests four levels of an approach with China... 1) curbing the most dangerous uses of AI... 2) agreeing to test models before release... 3) setting some kind of "speed limit" on the rate of recursive self-improvement (RSI); and 4) a full pacing, or even "pause"
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Amodei frames AI cooperation with China as instrumental to protecting the US and allied lead, warning that Chinese defection from any pacing agreement could hand China geopolitical dominance.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Even the safety-slowdown camp is framing cooperation in lead-preservation, not purely altruistic, terms — useful context for judging how far US policymakers will actually go in any China AI deal.
insights.quote: If China defects from an agreement with the West, "such a defection could lead to their geopolitical dominance [and that] we should approach any global pacing decision in such a way that protects the lead of the United States and its allies."
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: Trump has publicly called AI safety concerns a 'hoax' and rejected calls to slow AI development, leaving the US government with a laissez-faire stance on domestic AI regulation.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A president dismissing AI safety as a 'hoax' while his own Treasury Secretary quietly pursues narrow China AI-risk talks creates real policy incoherence risk that could blunt any summit-level AI announcement.
insights.quote: Trump has called concerns about AI safety a "hoax" and has rejected calls to slow down AI development.
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: US private-sector AI data center investment commitments may reach $2.4 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A $2.4 trillion data-center buildout figure is a scale marker for the AI capex cycle and for why the US government has strong incentive not to constrain the industry via international agreements.
insights.quote: US private sector commitments may run to $2.4 trillion by 2030 according to McKinsey.
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: The US and China have approximately zero mutual trust, and unlike Cold War-era nuclear arms control, US large language model and AI capability development sits with private corporations the government does not control, making any AI safety pact structurally harder than Reagan-Gorbachev-era arms control.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: The private-sector-control problem is a structural, not merely political, obstacle to any US-China AI pact — implying that voluntary industry self-restraint (like the Amodei essay) may matter more near-term than intergovernmental treaties.
insights.quote: nuclear weapons were not held by private corporations, whereas in the United States, that is where large language models and AI experimentation reside. The US government does not control this technology, has no experience in its regulation
insights.locator: possible cooperation on AI safeguards section

insights.claim: AI-guided drone swarms are already being used to strike Kyiv's electric grid and Russian petroleum facilities, illustrating AI's dual-use military and commercial applications.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: Active AI-guided drone warfare against critical infrastructure underscores why any US-China AI-safeguards deal would need to address military dual-use applications, not just civilian model releases.
insights.quote: The swarms of drones that lash out at Kiev's electric grid or Russian petroleum facilities are guided by AI.
insights.locator: dual-use section

insights.claim: A no-summit-breakthrough joint US-China AI cancer research 'moonshot' is not expected, despite China holding vast clinical, genetic, and patient registry data that could aid global cancer research, partly because the US administration has cut NIH research funding.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A missed opportunity for AI-enabled biomedical cooperation is flagged as a casualty of US domestic research-funding cuts, not just geopolitical distrust.
insights.quote: Don't expect a joint cancer moonshot being announced at this summit.
insights.locator: biomedical cooperation section

insights.claim: The Trump administration has terminated or frozen nearly 2,300 previously approved NIH research grants, pulling back roughly $2.5 billion in active biomedical research funding.
insights.speaker: Alan Wm. Wolff
insights.so_what: A concrete $2.5 billion / 2,300-grant NIH funding pullback quantifies the retrenchment in US biomedical research capacity, relevant to biotech and academic research funding outlooks.
insights.quote: The administration reportedly has successfully terminated or frozen nearly 2,300 previously approved NIH research grants, pulling back roughly $2.5 billion in active biomedical research funding.
insights.locator: biomedical cooperation section
